lines.text: Circe had warned him about what came next.
First, the Sirens. Two creatures who sat in a meadow beside the sea and sang.
Every sailor who heard them steered straight toward them, and the meadow around them was piled with bones, the skin still drying on them.
The crew plugged their ears with wax.
Odysseus, of course, wanted to hear it.
So he had them tie him to the mast, hand and foot, and he told them: if I beg you to untie me, tie me tighter.
The wind dropped and the sea went flat, and then they heard the song.
What they sang about was him.
Come here, famous Odysseus, glory of the Greeks.
We know everything you suffered at Troy, and everything that happens anywhere on earth.
Stop and listen, and you'll leave knowing more than you came with.
They'd picked the bait well.
They offered him his own fame and the chance to know everything, and those were the two things he wanted most.
He begged them to untie him.
He shouted and pulled at the ropes until they cut into his skin.
Two of his men got up and tied him tighter.
Slowly the song faded behind them.
They took the wax out of their ears and kept rowing, toward the narrowest place in the sea.
Odysseus had to sail through a strait that no ship had ever crossed whole.
On one side lived Charybdis, a whirlpool that swallowed the sea three times a day, and with it every ship that came too close.
On the other side, high on a cliff, lived Scylla, a monster with six long necks and six heads, each with three rows of teeth.
The witch Circe had warned him: you cannot fight her, and you cannot outrun them both. Choose one.
Charybdis would take the whole ship. Scylla would take six men.
So Odysseus made his choice, and he told his crew nothing.
He put on his armour, took two spears, and stood at the bow, as if he could protect them.
They steered toward the cliff, staring in terror at the whirlpool.
Then the six heads came down.
In a single moment, six of his best men were lifted into the air, screaming his name, reaching out to him.
And he could not save a single one.
The ship shot out of the strait, and the crew rowed on in silence.
Of everything he suffered on the long road home, it was the most pitiful thing he ever saw.
Ahead lay an island, green and quiet, and from the water they could hear cattle lowing.
Odysseus remembered the prophecy and told them they weren't landing. They'd sail straight past.
But his men were worn out.
Eurylochus stood up and said what all of them were thinking.
You're made of iron, Odysseus, and we aren't. Let us sleep one night on dry land.
Odysseus gave in, but he made every one of them swear an oath that nobody would touch the cattle.
That night a storm came, and after the storm the wind settled in the south, the one direction that couldn't carry them home.
It blew from there for a month.
They ate everything on the ship. They fished, and they hunted birds, and they starved anyway.
One day, while Odysseus was off alone praying, Eurylochus made a speech.
Every kind of death is terrible, he said, but starving is the worst.
Let's kill the best of the cattle and offer some to the gods.
And if the Sun is angry, I'd rather drown in one gulp than waste away on this island.
When Odysseus came back, he could smell the roasting meat from a long way off.
What happened next is the strangest scene in the poem.
The hides of the dead cattle crawled across the ground, and the meat on the spits mooed.
The Sun went to Zeus and told him to punish them.
If you don't, he said, I'll go down into the house of the dead and shine there instead.
When the wind finally changed, they sailed. As soon as the island dropped behind them, Zeus threw his thunderbolt.
The mast came down and crushed the helmsman's skull.
The ship filled with smoke and the stink of sulphur, and the men were thrown into the water.
For a while the waves carried them around the wreck like seabirds, and then they went under.
All of them.
Odysseus lashed the broken mast to the keel and held on, and all night the current dragged him back the way he'd come.
Back to the strait, and back to Charybdis.
When the whirlpool sucked his raft down, he jumped and grabbed a fig tree growing out of the cliff,
and he hung there like a bat all day, waiting for the sea to spit his wood back up.
Eventually it did. He dropped down onto it and paddled away with his hands.
He drifted for nine days.
